paragraphs.source_en: For once, the master formally set out from the front entrance in a rickshaw. After that, the master’s wife, having finished her breakfast as usual, immediately urged the children, “Hurry off to school, or you’ll be late.” The children, however, were perfectly calm and showed no sign of leaving. They said, “Why! Today is a holiday.” The master’s wife scolded them, “How could it be a holiday? Go on, quickly.” The eldest sister paid no attention at all and said, “But, but yesterday Teacher said it was a holiday.” Only then did the master’s wife find it somewhat odd; she took a calendar from the cupboard and checked it, and sure enough the day was printed in red and marked as a festival day. Most likely the master, not knowing today was a holiday, had deliberately sent a note of absence to the school, while his wife had absentmindedly dropped the letter into the mailbox. As for Meitei, however, whether he truly did not know it was a holiday or knew and deliberately kept silent remains impossible to say. The master’s wife, somewhat startled by this discovery, could only say to the children, “Since there’s no school, play quietly at home.” With that, she took out her sewing box as usual and began her needlework.

paragraphs.source_en: For the next half hour the household was peaceful, and nothing worth recording here took place. Then a strange visitor arrived, a schoolgirl of seventeen or eighteen. She wore leather shoes with crooked heels, dragged along a pair of purple hakama, and had her hair puffed out like abacus beads. Without so much as announcing herself, she came in through the back door. This was the master’s niece, a young lady with the quite pretty name of Yukie. She was said to be a student at a girls’ school; sometimes on Sundays she would come visiting, often quarrel with her uncle, and then go home. Of course, pretty though her name was, her looks were not so pretty as the name; walk a hundred or two meters down the street and one would surely meet a girl much like her.
